name: libjson (vincenthz)
workload: nativejson-benchmark serialisation of three in-memory trees (canada.json, citm_catalog.json, twitter.json) to condensed and prettified JSON strings, plus a DOM statistics traversal, libjson against nlohmann/json v2.0.3.
claimed_speedup: Stringify total 68.8 ms vs 87.7 ms for nlohmann (1.28x), prettify 69.3 ms vs 130.6 ms (1.88x), DOM statistics traversal 0.80 ms vs 2.17 ms (2.7x), parse memory 8.6 MB vs 9.9 MB (all ratios and totals derived from page data). Parse is slower: 107.2 ms vs 72.5 ms (0.68x). Per file stringify: canada 61.5 vs 76.3 ms, citm 4.07 vs 7.18 ms, twitter 3.19 vs 4.24 ms.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS; build/premake5.lua release configuration uses optimize Full (-O3 under gmake, assumed) plus buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra; library versions are the 2016 submodule snapshot (nlohmann v2.0.3, picojson 1.3.0)
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz
tradeoffs: Interruptible SAX-style (SAJ) parser and printer with no object model and no number conversion: the user supplies the tree and converts numbers. LGPL (header in json.c says version 2.1 or 3.0 only); the repo has no LICENSE file. Optional nesting and size limits, UTF-8 validation, comments, custom allocators. Build system is only meant for testing; the author recommends embedding the two source files.
caveats: The benchmark's tree (tree_create_structure, tree_append, tree_print and the statistics traversal in src/tests/vincenthzlibjsontest.cpp) is harness code written for the benchmark, because libjson has no DOM; the Stringify, Prettify and Statistics rows therefore time that harness tree plus libjson's printer, and the 2.7x statistics win says nothing about libjson itself. Parse, the one row that exercises libjson's parser building a tree, is slower than nlohmann/json (1.48x). libjson's own SAX rows have no nlohmann baseline (SAX round-trip 30.8 ms, SAX statistics 22.5 ms, versus RapidJSON 18.1 and 6.3 ms). Conformance in the same suite: 2 of 34 parse-validation, 9 of 66 double-parse and 10 of 27 round-trip tests fail. The README's 'Fast' claim itself has no numbers. Sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use 2016 library versions; nlohmann/json has changed a lot since v2.0.3, so today's ratios against it will differ. Per-library totals in claimed_speedup are sums of the three per-file rows (canada.json 2199KB, citm_catalog.json 1737KB, twitter.json 632KB) and are derived from page data.

name: libjson (SourceForge)
workload: mloskot/json_benchmark 'small' set: 500 sample JSON strings of 100-500 characters parsed into the library's DOM type, 1000 iterations, libjson against JsonCpp, RapidJSON, casablanca and JSON Spirit.
claimed_speedup: Visual C++ 11.0 32-bit: 1000 iterations of 500 parsings in 5.2787 to 5.29663 s for libjson vs 5.762 to 5.77978 s for JsonCpp (about 1.09x, derived from page data); libjson lazy-parsing mode 0.478065 to 0.486636 s (about 12x against JsonCpp's full parse, derived from page data, but lazy parsing defers work so it is not like-for-like). RapidJSON is faster than both at 0.961858 to 0.962361 s; large canada.json: libjson 240.289 s vs RapidJSON 7.97 s per 1000 parses (about 30x slower, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Visual C++ 11.0 (32-bit); 'optimised builds' built with Boost.Build 'b2 variant=release' (exact compiler flags not listed)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.10GHz, 16 GB RAM, Windows 7 64-bit
tradeoffs: C++ library with a C interface, lazy parsing, streaming and DOS protection options, many compile-time switches. Project page calls it 'super-effiecient and usually runs circles around other JSON libraries'.
caveats: Project page makes the directional claim without numbers; the only numbers are from an independent 2013 hobby benchmark that its author says is not maintained and was superseded by Native JSON Benchmark. On gcc 4.7 libjson was not measured, so the JsonCpp comparison exists only on the VC++ 32-bit run. The benchmark README does not say whether the lazy-mode line comes from that same run or which libjson build options were used. Large-document libjson result has no JsonCpp row. The SourceForge page and file pages I could open do not state a licence (licence tag in the awesome-cpp list is just 'libjson'), so usability is marked reference until the licence text is checked. This is a different project from vincenthz/libjson. Last update date is the SourceForge page's 'Last Update' (2016-11-09), not a verified commit date.

name: Parson
workload: nativejson-benchmark parse of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json into each library's DOM, Parson against JsonCpp, json-c and Qt QJsonDocument (and nlohmann/json v2.0.3 as the faster reference).
claimed_speedup: Parse total 89.5 ms vs JsonCpp 165.5 ms (1.85x), json-c 134.6 ms (1.50x), Qt QJsonDocument 125.0 ms (1.40x) (derived from page data); parse memory 9.1 MB vs JsonCpp 24.6 MB and json-c 49.9 MB (derived); prettify 111.2 ms vs nlohmann/json 130.6 ms (1.17x, derived). Per file parse: canada 64.6 ms vs JsonCpp 142.5 ms and json-c 105.8 ms. Slower than nlohmann/json on parse (89.5 vs 72.5 ms) and stringify (110.9 vs 87.7 ms), and than JsonCpp on stringify (110.9 vs 94.3 ms).
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS; build/premake5.lua release configuration uses optimize Full (-O3 under gmake, assumed) plus buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra; library versions are the 2016 submodule snapshot (nlohmann v2.0.3, picojson 1.3.0)
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz
tradeoffs: Two-file, C89-compatible DOM library with dot-notation access and a small memory footprint (about 2.7x less parse memory than JsonCpp in this run). Not a speed library: its own README makes no performance claim.
caveats: Nobody claims Parson is fast: the README has no performance claim and the wins are only against the slower incumbents JsonCpp, json-c and QJsonDocument; it loses to nlohmann/json, cJSON (24.7 ms parse total) and RapidJSON (7.9 ms). Conformance in the same suite: 3 of 34 parse-validation, 1 of 9 string-parse and 13 of 27 round-trip tests fail. Library revision used in the sample is not stated. Sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use 2016 library versions; nlohmann/json has changed a lot since v2.0.3, so today's ratios against it will differ. Per-library totals in claimed_speedup are sums of the three per-file rows (canada.json 2199KB, citm_catalog.json 1737KB, twitter.json 632KB) and are derived from page data.

name: PicoJSON
workload: nativejson-benchmark stringify of three DOMs (canada.json, citm_catalog.json, twitter.json) and a DOM statistics traversal, PicoJSON 1.3.0 against nlohmann/json v2.0.3 and JsonCpp.
claimed_speedup: Stringify total 80.2 ms vs 87.7 ms for nlohmann (1.09x) and 94.3 ms for JsonCpp (1.18x); DOM statistics traversal 0.89 ms vs 2.17 ms for nlohmann (2.4x) and 2.62 ms for JsonCpp (2.9x) (all derived from page data). Parse is slower than nlohmann: 140.3 ms vs 72.5 ms (0.52x) but 1.18x faster than JsonCpp's 165.5 ms (derived).
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS; build/premake5.lua release configuration uses optimize Full (-O3 under gmake, assumed) plus buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra; library versions are the 2016 submodule snapshot (nlohmann v2.0.3, picojson 1.3.0)
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Intel Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80GHz
tradeoffs: Header-only, dependency-free C++ JSON parser and serializer with STL-friendly types and pull or streaming interfaces; a small variant tree (picojson::value). No prettified-output row in the sample.
caveats: The README makes no performance claim; the only numbers are the third-party suite's. The wins are small (stringify 1.09x) or on a traversal of the library's own value type, and the library is about 2x slower than nlohmann/json at parsing. Conformance in the same suite: 4 of 34 parse-validation and 11 of 27 round-trip tests fail. Last commit is 2021-01-17, so the repo is treated as abandoned although the author has not said so. Sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use 2016 library versions; nlohmann/json has changed a lot since v2.0.3, so today's ratios against it will differ. Per-library totals in claimed_speedup are sums of the three per-file rows (canada.json 2199KB, citm_catalog.json 1737KB, twitter.json 632KB) and are derived from page data.

name: pugixml
workload: Automated Docker benchmark (bemayer/xml-benchmark, monthly GitHub Actions run of 2026-10-01): DOM parse (pugi::xml_document::load_string vs xmlParseMemory plus xmlFreeDoc), XPath query //*[@id], and serialize, on generated and real-world XML.
claimed_speedup: DOM parse of the 10.0 MB 'other' bucket (consistent with the README's real-world extracts): 26.0 ms vs 188.0 ms for libxml2 (7.2x), memory 51.1 MB vs 166.7 MB (3.3x less); 104 MB generated bucket: 124.8 ms vs 943.0 ms (7.6x), 324 vs 933 MB; 29 MB bucket: 23.5 vs 135.5 ms (5.8x); XPath //*[@id] on the 104 MB bucket: 24.2 ms vs 628.5 ms (26x); ratios derived from page data. Mixed elsewhere: serialize is 2.0x faster on the 104 MB bucket (107.7 vs 218.3 ms) and 2.8x on the 'other' bucket but libxml2 is 1.6x faster on the 29 MB bucket (20.2 vs 32.0 ms); libxml2 is slightly faster at DOM parse on the '1MB' bucket (13.9 vs 14.4 ms) and '100KB' bucket (1.25 vs 1.54 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Debian bookworm-slim g++ (version not pinned, 12.x inferred), CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (default Release flags, C++17); pugixml fetched from master (unpinned); libxml2 is the Debian bookworm package
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: DOM parser with in-situ parsing and XPath 1.0; non-validating, does less than libxml2 (no DTD or schema validation, no namespace-aware tree, no HTML mode). Source readme calls it 'an extremely fast XML parser'.
caveats: The project's own benchmark page (pugixml.org/benchmark.html: nine 1-20 MB files, ratios against pugixml, Visual Studio 2015, Core i7 @ 2.67 GHz per a search snippet) is behind the egress block here, so I could not open it; the numbers above come from an independent hobby repo whose results are embedded in the gh-pages index.html (opened via raw.githubusercontent.com, run dated 2026-10-01). Its size labels do not match the file sizes (implied size = throughput x time: the '100KB' bucket is 2.85 MB, '1MB' is 24.4 MB, '10MB' is 29.2 MB, '100MB' is 104 MB), neither program checks that the parse succeeded, and the '1MB' bucket shows 1.7 GB/s for both libraries, which suggests an early error exit (libxml2 has a default nesting limit of 256), so I quoted only the '10MB', '100MB' and real-world rows. The shared CI runner adds noise; the CPU model is unknown; the report omits RapidXML DOM rows. libxml2 also validates and tracks more than pugixml, so the work is not identical. A rival's table (mdz_xml README, Intel i5-6600, VC++ toolset v100, flags and harness not public) shows pugixml 800 MB parse in 1.24 s vs TinyXML-2 7.42 s (6.0x), MSXML 6.0 12.94 s (10.4x) and Rapid-XML 1.69 s (1.36x), derived from that page; first-party tier C evidence.
